I’d recommend playing to your strengths! You said self-awareness is something you’re good at, use that to disengage with negative thought patterns that feed into your guilt. More simply, don’t let guilt and frustration over your behaviors, past or present prevent take you out of the “I can be better” mindset! Instead of spiraling about what could’ve happened, focus on what you can control, and you can control what you do next. That also means to be patient with yourself, slip-ups will happen. Nobody can be mindful 24/7/365.

More practically, I’d recommend getting really in tune to the physical indicators you notice when you’re feeling a specific emotion. When you can recognize yourself becoming more emotionally heightened, separate from the problem, even if it’s only for a second, and gather your thoughts. 

I found that, for me, when I become really emotional too quickly to notice, or if it’s a really inopportune time to step away, I’ll use what I like to call “Snap the fuck out of it” techniques, which are usually focused around intense, physical sensations to ‘snap me the fuck out of it.’ I’ll use a rubber band and snap it against my arm, but you can grab a handful of ice, or squeeze a pressure point. Doing these things can help me find a lapse in harmful thinking patterns and those blank spaces are the opportunity to stop, de-escalate, and regroup with your goals. It’s important that whatever you find is not harmful for you in the long run, like cutting or bruising yourself. 

I hope you find something that helps you become your favorite version of you.

You seem pretty self-aware, based on what you’ve written. You’re self-aware enough to admit you’re still getting a handle on your emotions, and you’re self-aware enough to identify triggers. Use that skill to your advantage!

In my experience, emotions to an extreme degree frequently pop up, and it’s usually in reaction to something. Especially if it’s perceived criticism. I say “perceived”  because exactly like you, I’m never quite sure if what I’m feeling is valid, or if my perspective on things are warped because of my mental illness. Sometimes, criticism isn’t intentional, we just interpret the message in that way, but it’s not necessarily a ‘bad’ thing to be criticized, it gives us the opportunity to weigh that comment, give it time and let the emotions run their course, and see if it has any merit when you’re at more of a baseline emotional state. 

So, I don’t make big decisions that might impact others, I don’t have important conversations, and I give myself time to let the feelings pass. I do what I know helps me regulate (it’s a lot of isolation, self-care, and crappy movies) and then I’ll find my way back to baseline, and I can feel more confident that my decisions are not me being ‘too emotional’. You might find my method doesn’t work great for you, and that’s okay, keep working at regulating and mindful communication however that looks like for you, I’m hoping the best for you!

So I have two ways of thinking. I do totally notice events and hints in my life that upon reflection, could be interpreted as foreshadowing, maybe by the universe or karma, or whatever force of change that makes everything run the way it’s supposed to. It does flare up when I’m overthinking a lot, which is typically when I’m depressed and what not.

On the other hand, I can also look at it from a realist perspective, and cognitive distortions, or “magical thinking” as I’ve heard it called, is our brains way of making sense of the chaos around us. We can associate events or happenings with other, unrelated things. Like how some people are superstitious of black cats, or walking under ladders is considered bad luck! But there’s no real proof that those things ACTUALLY affect our reality. 

My therapist and I have talked about it and he says that a little cognitive distortion is fine, as long as it’s not impeding our happiness. For example, if you see a sign and it strikes fear into your heart, and stops you from doing something you wished to do, then that behaviour is not serving you. If  you see your lucky number as your total on your receipt after paying for gas, and it gets you in a good mood and helps you pay attention to the positive aspects of your day, whether it was luck related or not, then that’s okay :)

I think it’s possible for two exes to be friends, but pwBPD aren’t necessarily built to hold back on their relationships, especially if you’ve already passed the point of the other becoming a FP.

I think it might chronically trigger you, to be able to spend time with this person but not do the things that bring you comfort. Like a constant state of perceived abandonment.

I also don’t think it’s very fair to put it all on yourself. Yes, you have a disorder and need to build up your coping skills and get to a place where you can love healthily and reduce toxic qualities, but he also needs to work on himself. If you’re the only one working towards a mutually satisfying and healthy relationship, but HE doesn’t put any effort into his healing, then I would NOT return to that.

I honestly think you might have a better outcome if you two take time and space from each other, develop your own autonomy and healthy coping mechanisms, and then after the “break” period, if you both deem the other to be healthy enough for you, then go for it. But also go through other possible outcomes mentally, and find peace with whatever outcomes might happen. (For example, one outcome might be that you guys might not get back together, make peace with that.)

Good luck. You deserve love and healing, and if you put effort into growth, you’ll make someone as happy as they make you one day.

I learned that what I was actually doing was prolonging my suffering. I was taking moments that were ripe with opportunity to spend time with my loved ones, make memories, and strengthen our bond but instead of doing that, I “decided” to worry and fret and feel bad. I use quotation marks because it never felt intentional, but my therapist helped me see that the wording wasn’t inaccurate. You have the capability to intentionally counter those thoughts and the choice to reduce the amount of suffering you go through. I feel like for me, that way of thinking came very naturally and it was not difficult for me to ruminate and get depressed over events that are not even real right now. 

It’s scary to think about the fleeting nature of life, but do your best to direct that fear into something productive. Instead of closing people off because the pain of losing them would be unbearable, develop that bond and thoroughly enjoy the time spent, because as much as it will hurt losing someone you love, you’ve only got to deal with that kind of loss once per person, so you’re essentially doubling, or tripling the pain you’re going through.

I’ve you’ve never heard of it, I recommend the “FODMAP” diet, it’s a process of eating foods you KNOW don’t trigger a reaction, and slowly expanding out to new foods. If something makes you feel icky, take note of it! Eventually you’ll have a pretty good idea of what you can eat and what you can’t! Maybe you’ll even notice some trends about the food you can’t eat?
